title: Reprice open ferry bookings
prompt:
A ferry operator publishes a new fare sheet each season. Every booking that has not sailed yet must be charged the new fare for its route and cabin class.

Write one statement that sets bookings.fare to the fare_sheet fare for the same route and cabin, but only for bookings whose status is 'open'.

- The check runs SELECT id, fare FROM bookings after your SQL
- Bookings with status 'sailed' keep their fare
- An open booking with no matching (route, cabin) row in fare_sheet keeps its fare; never set it to NULL
- A match needs both route and cabin to be equal
- Any row order is fine
hints: You are updating one table using values from another. Which UPDATE form lets you join?
UPDATE bookings b SET fare = f.fare FROM fare_sheet f WHERE ... only touches rows that find a match.
UPDATE bookings b SET fare = f.fare FROM fare_sheet f WHERE f.route = b.route AND f.cabin = b.cabin AND b.status = 'open';

exercise.schema:
CREATE TABLE fare_sheet (route text NOT NULL, cabin text NOT NULL, fare numeric(7,2) NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (route, cabin));
CREATE TABLE bookings (id int PRIMARY KEY, route text NOT NULL, cabin text NOT NULL, status text NOT NULL, fare numeric(7,2) NOT NULL);
exercise.starter:
-- Apply the new fare sheet to open bookings
SELECT 1;
exercise.solution:
UPDATE bookings b
SET fare = f.fare
FROM fare_sheet f
WHERE f.route = b.route
  AND f.cabin = b.cabin
  AND b.status = 'open';

hiddenTests.name: cabin row on another route is not used
hiddenTests.seed:
INSERT INTO fare_sheet VALUES ('R1', 'cabin', 70.00), ('R2', 'deck', 11.00);
INSERT INTO bookings VALUES (1, 'R2', 'cabin', 'open', 50.00), (2, 'R1', 'deck', 'open', 12.00);

explanation: UPDATE ... FROM joins the target to fare_sheet and only updates bookings that find a matching row, so bookings with no fare stay as they are. The join must use both route and cabin; joining on route alone matches several fare rows and Postgres picks one of them unpredictably. The trap is the correlated-subquery form SET fare = (SELECT f.fare FROM fare_sheet f WHERE ...) without a WHERE EXISTS guard: it writes NULL (here, it fails the NOT NULL constraint) for unmatched bookings. Forgetting the status filter reprices bookings that already sailed.
notes: Because fare_sheet has a primary key on (route, cabin), each booking matches at most one row and the update is deterministic. Postgres writes a new row version for every updated row, even when the fare does not change; adding AND b.fare IS DISTINCT FROM f.fare skips those writes and reduces bloat. The SQL-standard alternative is MERGE INTO bookings USING fare_sheet ... WHEN MATCHED AND status = 'open' THEN UPDATE.
followUps: How would you return the old and new fare for each changed booking in the same statement?
What happens if fare_sheet had no primary key and contained two rows for the same route and cabin?
